n: Israel had no chariot army of its own. Facing larger, better-equipped enemies, their confidence rested on the God who had already defeated Egypt.
Before battle, a priest would address the troops. War in Israel was first a spiritual matter.
The priest’s message begins like the Shema — “Hear, O Israel” — and piles up four ways of saying “don’t be afraid.”
The reason for courage: the Lord himself goes with them and fights for them.

f.w: the LORD your God is he that goeth with you

n: Officers then announced exemptions. A man with a newly built house he hadn’t yet lived in could go home.

f.g: Hasn’t begun to live in it or formally opened it.

n: A man whose new vineyard hadn’t yet produced its first harvest for him could also return.

f.w: hath not yet eaten of it

n: A man engaged but not yet married was sent home so he wouldn’t die before starting his family.

f.g: Engaged — a legally binding promise to marry.

n: Even the fearful were sent home, so their fear wouldn’t spread. Gideon later used this very rule.
Only after the exemptions were commanders appointed to lead the remaining army.
When attacking a distant city, Israel must first offer terms of peace.
If the city surrendered, its people were spared but became subject laborers paying tribute.

f.g: People who pay tribute or provide forced labor.

n: If the city refused and fought, Israel could lay siege.

f.g: Surround a city to force surrender.

n: After victory, the fighting men were killed — a harsh custom of ancient warfare.

f.g: Refers to men capable of fighting.

n: Women, children, animals, and goods were spared and taken as spoils of war.
These rules applied to distant cities outside Canaan proper.
The cities of Canaan itself were treated differently: no one was to be left alive.

f.w: thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth

n: The six Canaanite peoples were placed under the ban (ḥerem). Many readers find this deeply troubling; the text explains it as judgment on extreme wickedness and protection of Israel’s faith.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — devote to God by destruction.

n: The stated reason: so Israel wouldn’t learn their detestable religious practices, such as child sacrifice. Sadly, incomplete obedience later led to exactly this.

f.w: That they teach you not to do after all their abominations

n: During a long siege, Israel must not cut down fruit trees. Trees aren’t enemy soldiers; they sustain human life. An early environmental protection.

f.w: the tree of the field is man's life
f.g: The Hebrew can be read as a question: “Is the tree of the field a man, that it should be besieged by you?”

n: Non-fruit trees could be used to build siege works against the enemy city.

f.g: Trees for food — “meat” in KJV means food in general.
